chunks: What is stack overflow?. The question: What is stack overflow?
The stack is a region of memory where the computer keeps track of the functions (named pieces of a program) running right now.
Every call adds one block, and every return removes one. A stack overflow happens when the blocks pile up past the memory reserved for the stack.
Common causes are a function that keeps calling itself, or a very large list of values declared inside a function. A big computer stops the program with an error.
A small chip often keeps going and silently damages other data.
Picture a plate dispenser in a cafeteria, a well of fixed depth. Each call puts a plate on top, and each return takes the top plate off. Pile on too many and they overflow.
On a PC, a solid wall sits at the bottom of the well, so you notice at once.
On a small chip, the well sits right next to your other belongings, and extra plates silently knock them over.
Each recursive call adds one frame below the previous one. The stack pointer (SP) walks toward low addresses.
When it crosses the end of the allocated region, a system with a guard page faults immediately; a system without one lets it silently overwrite whatever is next.
Stack frame: the block for one call. It holds the return address (where to go back to) and that function's local variables.
Stack pointer: a register (a tiny storage slot in the processor) that marks the current top of the stack. Recursion: a function that calls itself.
Guard page: a protected piece of memory just past the stack that triggers an error if touched.
A recursive function uses 48 bytes per call. A PC with an 8 MB stack fits about 8 388 608 over 48 about 175 000 nested calls.
The next call touches the guard page, and the program stops with an error. A small chip with a 2 KB stack and 24 bytes per call fits only about 2048 over 24 about 85 calls.
With no guard, call 86 silently overwrites whatever sits next to the stack. That is the whole idea.
"A stack overflow is when the call stack outgrows the region of memory reserved for it.
Each function call pushes a frame with the return address and locals, so very deep or infinite recursion, or big local arrays, can push the stack pointer past the limit.
On a PC the OS has a guard page, so you get a segfault. On a microcontroller with no MMU it silently overwrites globals or the heap.
You prevent it by avoiding unbounded recursion, keeping big buffers off the stack, and measuring the stack high-water mark."
